la:adv:diu.html:
dĭū (old form dĭūs, Orell. Inscr. 8206), adv.
old acc. form of duration of time; root in dies; v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 232 sqq.
.
(Acc. to dies, I. B. 2.) By day (very rare), ; usually with noctu: noctuque et diu,: noctu diuque, Titin. and Fragm. ap. P. ( Dietsch); ; ; : nec noctu, nec diu, Plaut. Fragm. ap. : diu noctuque iter properabunt,: noctu diuque hostibus obniti,.—
(Acc. to dies, II. A. 3.; lit., a space of time, a while; hence, with intens. signif.) A long time, long while, long (freq. in all periods; cf.: pridem, dudum): nimis diu et longum loquor,; cf. so with longum,: diu multumque scriptitare,; so, diu multumque,; ; ; ; ; also: multum diuque,: multum et diu,; : multum ac diu,; cf. also: recordatus multum et diu cogitavi ... Eam rem volutavi et diu disputavi, and 4: saepe et diu,; cf.: saepe diuque,; diu diuque,; , p. 266, 16: diu atque acriter pugnatum est,; et saep.: diu ego hunc cruciabo,: Stoici diu mansuros aiunt animos: semper, negant,. 31 fin.:

diu princeps oratorum, aliquando aemulus Ciceronis, : tam diu restitisti,: tam diu,; ; ; ; : eo, quo jam diu Sum judicatus,; so, jam diu,; ; ; cf.: diu est jam,: ille vult diu vivere, hic diu vixit: quamquam, O di boni! quid est in hominis vita diu? and 69; cf.: sat diu vixisse,: nimis diu maceror,; so, nimis diu,; : non diu apud hunc servies,; cf.: haud diu,; .—Followed by dum, donec: diu expectare, dum, etc.,: diu jacere donec, etc.,.—Comp.: diūtius, longer [the t inserted, as in sectius and setius from secus, being a remnant of adv. ending -ter or -tus]: nolo te jactari diutius,; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.: cf.: minus diu quam,.—In the historians freq. = a long while, very long, no comparison being intended: ne diutius commeatu prohiberetur,; ; ; 4, 35, 2; 7, 20, 5 et saep.: neque illis, qui victoriam adepti forent, diutius ea uti licuisset,: legiones diutius sine consulari fuere,.—Sup.: (Cato) qui senex diutissime fuisset,; so ; ; ; : ut quam diutissime te jucunda opinione oblectarem,; so with quam,.—

Long since, a great while ago (mostly ante-class.): quod arci, diu facti, celeriter corruissent, Varr. ap. ; cf.: scelus, inquam, factum'st jam diu antiquom et vetus,; so, jam diu,; ; ; ; ; for which: diu jam,; : is ex Anactorio ... huc commigravit in Calydonem haud diu,not long ago, a short time ago,: nec loci gnara sum, nec diu hic fui,it is not long since I was here,: jam diu est factum, quom discesti ab hero,.—With foll. quom, .— With postquam,.—With quod, ; Prol.—
In Mela repeatedly of place, a long way: Italia ... inter superum mare et inferum excurrit diu solida,; so ; . Cf. Hand Turs. II. pp. 285-291.

la:adj:diuturnus.html:
dĭūturnus, a, um (diŭ-, ), adj.
diu
,
of long duration, lasting, long (class.; cf.: diutinus, longinquus): quid putet in rebus humanis diuturnum, qui cognoverit, quid sit aeternum?; cf. gloria (opp. aeterna),; opp. extremum,: usus,: injuria,: bellum,: pax,; : quies,: labor,: obsidio,: mala, et saep.: status rei publicae,; cf. res publica,; 2, 3: rex,: non potes esse diuturnus,i. e. your power,: dux,experienced, veteran,.—Comp.: equae,longerlived,; cf. filia,; : molestiae,of longer duration,: impunitas,: multa,.—Sup.: poenae diuturnissimae, , 21, 23 init.—Adv.: diūturne, Orell. (dub. al. diuturnam).—Comp.: diuturnius,longer,; .

la:adj:diurnus.html:
dĭurnus, a, um, adj.
for dius-nus, from dies; cf.: interdius, quotidianus, etc.
,
of or belonging to the day.
In a wider sense, daily (perh. not ante-Aug.): aetatis fata diurna,i. e. of only one day,: instituit, ut tam Senatus quam populi diurna acta confierent et publicarentur,daily transactions, records, journal,; ; Oud. N. cr.; in the same signif.: commentarii,; cf. also: diurna actorum scriptura,. (Concerning these acta diurna, v. Lips. Exc. ad ; Ernest. Exc. ad ; Rupert. ad ; Walch ad , and the art. acta): cibus,daily allowance, rations,: victus,: mercede diurna conductus,.—Hence, subst.
diurnum, i, n., an account-book, day-book: longum,; plur. (sc. acta), diaries, records, minutes: diurna populi Romani, per provincias curatius leguntur,.—Also subst.
diurnum, i, n. (sc. frumentum), a daily portion, allowance, rations (cf. diarium), ; ; cf. .—
In a stricter sense (acc. to dies, I. B. 2.), opp. nocturnus, by day, of the day (very freq. and class.): diurnum nocturnumve spatium,: labores diurni nocturnique,; cf. so opp. nocturnus,; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.: lumen,; so ; cf. stella,i. e. the morning-star,: currus,i. e. the chariot of the sun,: ignes,: nitor,: actus,the day's business,.— Adv.: dĭurne, daily, ; .
